Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.full_text: ISSN(Print): 2373-3403 ISSN(Online): 2373-3411 Article Versions Export Article Cite this article - Normal Style - MLA Style - APA Style - Chicago Style Research Article Open Access Peer-reviewed Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry. 2026, 14(1), 1-14. DOI: 10.12691/jpbpc-14-1-1 Received September 07, 2026; Revised October 09, 2026; Accepted October 16, 2026 The identification of small molecules capable of interacting with multiple therapeutically relevant protein targets is an important strategy in early-stage drug discovery. In the present study, the Schiff base ligand ((N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine; N1) was computationally evaluated against a panel of representative disease-associated proteins to investigate its target-binding profile. The primary focus was the assessment of N1 against breast cancer-associated receptor kinases, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which play central roles in oncogenic signaling pathways. In addition, the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was included as an exploratory antiviral target to examine the broader target recognition capability of the ligand rather than to propose a common therapeutic mechanism. Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina with experimentally determined protein structures obtained from the Protein Data Bank. N1 demonstrated favorable binding affinities toward all investigated breast cancer targets, with docking scores of â8.708 kcal/mol for EGFR, â8.836 kcal/mol for HER2, â8.906 kcal/mol for VEGFR2, and â9.066 kcal/mol for PI3K. The ligand also exhibited a docking score of â8.8 kcal/mol against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein. Interaction analysis revealed multiple stabilizing hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, electrostatic interactions, and Ï-mediated interactions within the respective binding pockets.Drug-likeness assessment indicated compliance with Lipinski's and Ghose's rules, while ADMET prediction suggested favorable absorption and membrane permeability. Nevertheless, the predicted risks of hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and mutagenicity indicate that further structural optimization and experimental validation are required. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of N1 as a promising scaffold for breast cancer-associated kinase inhibition while providing preliminary evidence of its broader protein-binding capability across biologically distinct targets. Cancer and viral infections remain among the most serious global health challenges due to their high mortality rates, rapid disease progression, and limited availability of effective therapeutic agents 1, 2. Among different malignancies, breast cancer is one of the most frequently diagnosed cancers and represents a leading cause of cancer-related death among women worldwide 3. The development and progression of breast cancer are closely associated with abnormal activation of receptor tyrosine kinases and intracellular signaling proteins, particularly Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2), Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2 (VEGFR2), and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) 4, 5, 6. These signaling proteins regulate essential cellular processes such as proliferation, angiogenesis, migration, metastasis, survival, and apoptosis. Overexpression or mutation of these targets has been strongly linked with aggressive tumor progression and poor clinical prognosis 7. EGFR and HER2 activation initiates downstream signaling cascades, including the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which contribute to uncontrolled cancer cell proliferation, enhanced survival, and metastatic progression (Figure 1) 8, 9. VEGFR2 plays a crucial role in tumor angiogenesis by stimulating endothelial cell migration and vascular formation necessary for tumor growth and metastasis 10. PI3K, a central component of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, regulates cellular growth, proliferation, metabolism, and survival and is frequently dysregulated in breast cancer 11. Collectively, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K represent interconnected signaling proteins that regulate complementary aspects of breast cancer progression, including cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Since these proteins belong to functionally linked oncogenic signaling networks, their simultaneous computational evaluation provides an opportunity to investigate whether a single chemical scaffold can potentially interact with multiple biologically relevant targets involved in breast cancer. It should be noted that the present study aims to explore the binding characteristics of N1 toward these proteins through molecular docking and does not imply experimentally validated inhibition of these signaling pathways. Therefore, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K were selected as representative breast cancer-associated targets for an exploratory computational target-profiling study (Figure 1) 8, 9, 10, 11. In addition to cancer, viral infections caused by emerging and re-emerging viruses continue to pose major public health concerns worldwide. Andes hantavirus, a member of the Hantaviridae family, is responsible for hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe respiratory disease associated with high fatality rates 12. The viral nucleoprotein (N protein) plays an essential role in viral RNA encapsidation, ribonucleoprotein complex formation, genome replication, and viral assembly, making it a biologically relevant target for antiviral drug discovery (Figure 2) 13. Unlike viral enzymes, the nucleoprotein does not possess catalytic activity; instead, its RNA-binding region is responsible for recognizing and stabilizing viral genomic RNA during ribonucleoprotein assembly. Accordingly, the molecular docking analysis in the present study focused on this functionally important RNA-binding region to evaluate the potential molecular recognition of N1. Binding at this site may theoretically interfere with RNA recognition or ribonucleoprotein assembly; however, such effects remain computational hypotheses that require experimental validation 13, 14. The inclusion of the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was intended as an exploratory assessment of the binding versatility of the N1 scaffold against a structurally unrelated viral target rather than to propose a unified therapeutic strategy linking breast cancer and hantavirus infection. Despite the severe pathogenicity associated with hantavirus infections, currently available antiviral therapies remain limited, emphasizing the continuing need to identify new antiviral scaffolds for future investigation 14. In the present work, we report the synthesis and computational evaluation of a novel nitrothiophene-derived Schiff base ligand (N1). The primary objective of this study was to investigate its interaction with multiple breast cancer-associated kinase targets, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which collectively regulate tumor proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis. As an exploratory extension of this computational investigation, the ligand was also docked against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein to assess whether this chemical scaffold exhibits potential binding capability toward a structurally unrelated viral protein involved in RNA encapsidation. This exploratory comparison should not be interpreted as evidence of a unified therapeutic strategy but rather as an initial computational assessment of the molecular recognition properties of N1 across biologically distinct protein targets. The ligand (N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine, and its in silico activities are reported here for the first time. - Figure 1. The figure illustrates the proposed mechanism of action of the investigated ligand against major breast cancer-associated signaling proteins, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K. Activation of EGFR and HER2 normally initiates downstream signaling cascades such as the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which promote cancer cell proliferation, survival, and metastasis. VEGFR2 activation stimulates angiogenic signaling pathways responsible for tumor vascularization and endothelial cell migration. In the proposed mechanism, inhibition of these receptors suppresses phosphorylation-mediated signaling events, thereby reducing tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastatic progression. PI3K inhibition further decreases AKT/mTOR signaling, leading to apoptosis induction and suppression of cancer cell survival. Overall, the figure demonstrates the multi-target inhibitory action of the ligand against critical pathways involved in breast cancer progression - Figure 2. The figure represents the life cycle of Andes hantavirus and the proposed antiviral mechanism of the investigated compound targeting the viral nucleoprotein (N protein). The hantavirus initially enters the host cell through receptor-mediated endocytosis, followed by viral uncoating and release of ribonucleoprotein complexes into the cytoplasm. Viral RNA transcription and replication are subsequently carried out by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, leading to synthesis of viral proteins and assembly of new virions. The proposed ligand is suggested to bind within the RNA-binding region of the hantavirus nucleoprotein, thereby interfering with viral RNA encapsidation and ribonucleoprotein complex formation. This inhibition may suppress viral replication, reduce formation of mature viral particles, and prevent further viral dissemination within host cells. The overall antiviral outcome includes inhibition of viral replication, reduction of viral load, and prevention of hantavirus propagation 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Synthesis: Material All starting materials and solvents used were purchased from Aldrich and Fluka and were used without further purification. Melting points were determined in an open capillary tube on a Gallenkamp (Variable heater) melting point apparatus. NMR spectrum (1H) was recorded on an analysis X-685 benchtop NMR spectrophotometer at 60 MHz DMSO-d6 with TMS as internal standard, at the central science laboratory, Covenant University, Ota. The infrared spectra of all synthesized products were obtained using Agilent Cary 630 FTIR. The electronic spectra, of all the compounds, were obtained in solution, in the wavelength range 400-1000 nm using 1800 Shimadzu ultra-violet spectrophotometer. Both were carried out at the central science laboratory, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife. 2.2. Synthesis; Experimental An ethanolic solution of 1,8-diaminonaphthalene (0.83 g, 5.00 mmol) was introduced to a solution of 5-nitro-2-carboxaldehyde (1.62 g, 10.0 mmol) in absolute ethanol (25 mL) supplemented with glacial acetic acid (3 drops) as a catalyst. The reaction mixture was subjected to reflux conditions for 4 hours under atmospheric pressure. Following thermal treatment, the reaction vessel was allowed to equilibrate to ambient temperature, after which the volatile organic solvent was removed via rotary evaporation under reduced pressure until precipitation of a solid product occurred. The crude material was subsequently triturated with cold ethanol and subjected to recrystallization from a chloroform/ethanol solvent mixture (volume ratio 30:70). A deep orange-colored solid was obtained, collected by vacuum filtration, and dried under reduced pressure at 60Â°C until constant mass was achieved, yielding N1 as the isolated product. The compound demonstrated appreciable solubility in chloroform, ethanol, and methanol. The schematic representation for the preparation of N1 is given in Scheme 1. Yield: 1.49 g, 68.78%; m.p: 165ËC - 166ËC (d); IR (cmâ1): 1608 Î1⁄2(C=C), 1587 Î1⁄2(C=N), 1423 Î1⁄2(C=C, thiophene aromatic ring) 1490 and 1326 Î1⁄2(NO2), UV-Vis (nm): 299; 1 H NMR (60 MHz): DMSO-d6 Î ́ 7.95 (s, 1H), 7.21, 7.04 (d, 6H), 6.64, 6.55 (d, 2H). - Scheme 1. Schematic representation of the synthesis pathway of the novel Schiff base ligand N1, (N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine formed through the condensation reaction between 5-nitrothiophene-2-carbaldehyde and naphthalene-1,8-diamine. The figure also illustrates the optimized three-dimensional molecular structure of the synthesized compound2.3. Retrieval of Protein Structures The three-dimensional crystal structures of the selected therapeutic targets associated with breast cancer and viral infection were retrieved from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). The protein structures used in this study included epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR, PDB ID: 1M17, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2, PDB ID: 3PP0), vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2, PDB ID: 1YWN), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K, PDB ID: 4JPS), and Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein (PDB ID: 5E04 ). The biologically relevant protein chain (Chain A) was selected for all docking studies. These structures were chosen based on their high crystallographic resolution and the presence of co-crystallized ligands within the active site, allowing accurate definition of the ligand-binding pocket for molecular docking. 2.4. Protein Preparation Protein preparation was performed using AutoDock Tools. Prior to docking, all crystallographic water molecules, co-crystallized ligands, and non-essential heteroatoms were removed while preserving the protein backbone and active-site residues. Polar hydrogen atoms were subsequently added, and Kollman united-atom partial charges were assigned to the protein structures. The prepared receptors were saved in PDBQT format for docking calculations 19. 2.5. Ligand Preparation The chemical structure of the synthesized ligand was generated using ChemDraw Professional 12.0 and converted into a three-dimensional structure using Avogadro . Geometry optimization was carried out using the MMFF94 force field until convergence to obtain a minimum-energy conformation. Hydrogen atoms were added, appropriate protonation corresponding to physiological pH (approximately 7.4) was assigned, and Gasteiger partial atomic charges were calculated using AutoDock Tools. The optimized ligand was finally converted into PDBQT format for molecular docking 20, 21. 2.6. Molecular Docking Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina (version 1.2.7) to evaluate the binding affinity and binding mode of the ligand against the selected protein targets. The docking grid was centered on the active-site region defined by the co-crystallized ligand in each receptor structure. A grid box of 25 Ã 25 Ã 25 Ã with a grid spacing of 1.0 Ã was employed to adequately encompass the entire binding pocket. Docking calculations were carried out using an exhaustiveness value of 8, and 10 binding poses were generated for each protein-ligand complex. The resulting docking conformations were ranked according to their predicted binding free energies (kcal/mol). The optimal binding pose for each complex was selected based on the lowest binding free energy together with a favorable binding orientation and the formation of key interactions with biologically relevant active-site residues identified from the corresponding crystal structures and supported by previous literature 22, 23. 2.7. Drug-Likeness Evaluation The drug-likeness properties of N1 were evaluated using widely accepted computational pharmacokinetic filters, including Lipinskiâs Rule of Five and Ghoseâs filter, to assess its suitability as a potential orally active therapeutic agent. Physicochemical parameters such as molecular weight, hydrogen bond acceptors, hydrogen bond donors, partition coefficient (logP), molar refractivity, and total number of atoms were calculated to determine the drug-like behavior and oral bioavailability of the compound 24, 25. Lipinskiâs Rule of Five was applied based on the criteria of molecular weight below 500 Da, hydrogen bond acceptors fewer than 10, hydrogen bond donors fewer than 5, and logP value below 5, which are considered favorable for oral drug candidates 24. In addition, Ghoseâs filter was employed to further evaluate the compound by considering acceptable ranges of molecular weight, lipophilicity, molar refractivity, and atom count commonly associated with biologically active molecules 25. All calculations and predictions were performed using an online ADMET and drug-likeness prediction platform. The obtained parameters were analyzed to determine the compliance of N1 with established drug-likeness criteria 2.8. ADMET Prediction Studies ADMET (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity) prediction studies are extensively utilized in modern drug discovery to evaluate the pharmacokinetic behavior, bioavailability, and toxicity profile of potential therapeutic molecules prior to experimental and clinical investigations 26, 27. ADMET analysis assists in identifying compounds with favorable absorption, distribution, metabolic stability, elimination characteristics, and reduced toxicity, thereby minimizing the risk of late-stage drug failure and reducing the overall cost and time required for drug development 28. In the present study, ADMET prediction of N1 was performed using the admetSAR web server. Parameters associated with intestinal absorption, bloodâbrain barrier permeability, cytochrome P450 metabolism, excretion behavior, and different toxicity endpoints were evaluated to determine the pharmacological suitability and safety profile of N1 as a potential anticancer and antiviral therapeutic candidate 29, 30. 3. analysis.summary_en: Background: The study addresses the need for small molecules that can bind multiple disease‑relevant proteins, focusing on breast cancer kinases and Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein, which are major health challenges. Methods: The Schiff base ligand N1 was evaluated by molecular docking with AutoDock Vina using experimentally determined protein structures from the Protein Data Bank for EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, PI3K, and the hantavirus nucleoprotein. Results: N1 showed docking scores of –8.708 kcal/mol (EGFR), –8.836 kcal/mol (HER2), –8.906 kcal/mol (VEGFR2), –9.066 kcal/mol (PI3K) and –8.8 kcal/mol against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein, with multiple stabilizing interactions identified. Contribution: The findings suggest N1 as a promising scaffold for multi‑target breast cancer kinase inhibition and provide preliminary evidence of its broader protein‑binding capability, informing future drug‑discovery efforts. Limitations: The study is purely computational, lacks experimental validation, and predicts potential hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and mutagenicity requiring further optimization.

papers.title: From Systemic Inflammation to Calcium Leak: The RyR2 Hypothesis of Reversible Myocardial Dysfunction in Andes Virus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes virus is a severe zoonotic disease characterized by a paradoxical cardiac phenotype: profound myocardial dysfunction that is frequently reversible in survivors and occurs without extensive structural damage. The mechanisms linking systemic inflammation to this reversible dysfunction remain unknown. This review examines the hypothesis that inflammatory signaling converges on the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2), a major intracellular Ca2+-release channel, through post-translational modifications, generating reversible myocardial dysfunction in HCPS. analysis.background: HCPS caused by Andes virus shows profound but often reversible myocardial dysfunction without extensive structural damage (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The review proposes that systemic inflammation converges on the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2) via post‑translational modifications, linking cytokines, ROS/RNS to Ca2+ leak (A3).
analysis.current_state: Experimental models demonstrate that elevated IL‑6, oxidative and nitrosative stress activate CaMKII‑dependent phosphorylation, cysteine oxidation, and S‑nitrosylation of RyR2, destabilizing the channel and producing diastolic Ca2+ leak (A4).
analysis.gaps: The exact causal pathway from inflammation to RyR2 dysfunction in patients is unproven, and no specific therapy exists (A2).
analysis.future_research: Research should evaluate RyR2‑stabilizing drugs (rycals), optimal timing of intervention, and validate the hypothesis in animal models and HCPS patient cohorts (A7).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS caused by Andes virus shows profound but often reversible myocardial dysfunction without extensive structural damage (A1). analysis_zh.background: 由 安第斯病毒 引起的汉坦病毒心肺综合征表现出深度但常可逆的心肌功能障碍,且无广泛的结构性损伤 (A1)。

papers.title: Hantaviral therapeutics: life cycle targets and chemotherapeutic interventions
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses represent a persistent global health threat, being responsible for life-threatening diseases such as Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS). Despite high case fatality rates and recent outbreaks, there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines. Clinical management remains heavily reliant on supportive care and repurposed drugs, which often exhibit limited efficacy and dose-limiting toxicities. This review examines rational drug design strategies targeting critical steps in the viral life cycle, specifically Gn/Gc-mediated cellular entry and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)-driven genome replication. We evaluate the current landscape of viral inhibitors, including peptidomimetics, nucleoside analogues, and naturally derived compounds. To accelerate the discovery of novel treatments, we advocate for the integration of modern in silico screening to evaluate extensive chemical and natural product libraries. These broad compound collections offer a structurally diverse and largely untapped reservoir for antiviral development. Ultimately, expanding preclinical testing to include globally neglected variants will be essential to develop broad-spectrum hantaviral therapeutics capable of mitigating future epidemic threats.
papers.journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology

papers.title: Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavirus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisector collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting-specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before harvest periods in endemic agricultural regions.

Medically impor- tant hantaviruses are maintained primarily in rodent reservoirs and are associated with two major human disease syndromes: haemorrhagic fever with renal syn- drome (HFRS), reported mainly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also his- torically referred to as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome), reported mainly in the Americas [1–3]. Human infec- tion is usually accidental and occurs when people enter environments contaminated by infectious rodent excreta; however, Andes virus remains the major exception, with documented person-to-person transmission under con- ditions of close or prolonged contact [3, 4]. Rather than cataloguing hantavirus species, this review focuses on synthesising the evidence for how ecological *Correspondence: Xinyu Wang snowmed@gmail.com 1 Department of Infectious Diseases, Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai 200040, China 2 National Medical Center for Infectious Diseases, Shanghai 200040, China Page 2 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 and social processes shape human infection. Key ques- tions are not only which virus is carried by which rodent, but under what environmental and behavioural condi- tions infected reservoirs and susceptible humans are brought into contact. This framing is relevant for the One Health approach, because hantavirus risk can be exam- ined across measurable links including the rodent popu- lation density, reservoir-infection prevalence, climate variability, land use, agricultural or occupational expo- sure, housing conditions, recreational travel and clinical surveillance [1, 5]. China’s long-standing HFRS experi- ence, Europe’s cyclic Puumala virus epidemics and HCPS outbreaks in the Americas collectively provide comple- mentary evidence for understanding hantavirus emer- gence as an integrated human–animal–environment problem. This makes hantavirus disease a useful case for examining how the One Health approach can move from a conceptual framework to measurable surveillance indi- cators and setting-specific prevention. Reservoir ecology and environmental drivers of hantavirus risk The geographic distribution of hantavirus infection is strongly affected by its reservoir-host ecology. Although an increasing variety of hantaviruses have been detected in mammals, medically important hantaviruses are mainly maintained in rodent reservoirs, and many patho- genic viruses show close associations with particular host species or host complexes [1, 2]. This host dependence helps to explain the geographically uneven hantavirus risk, with human disease only occurring where compe- tent reservoirs, suitable habitats and human exposure all overlap. However, reservoir presence alone is insuf- ficient to predict human risk, and the local incidence also depends on rodent abundance, infection prevalence within reservoir populations, seasonal movement, habi- tat disturbance and the frequency with which humans enter contaminated environments [5]. Environmental variability can influence hantavirus transmission by changing the reservoir-host population dynamics and human–rodent contact. Increased rain- fall may enhance vegetation growth and food availabil- ity for rodents, thus supporting their reproduction and survival, while drought, habitat disruption or cold stress may drive rodents into human dwellings, storage areas or workplaces. The Four Corners region of the southwestern United States remains a classic example, where El Niño- associated precipitation led to ecological conditions that favoured increases in deer mouse populations, with a subsequent marked increase in HCPS cases in affected areas [6]. In Europe, Puumala virus epidemics have been linked to bank vole population cycles influenced by for- est ecology, food availability and seasonal conditions [7]. These examples suggest that climate is not a direct cause in isolation, but can influence risk via reservoir ecology and exposure pathways. Because human hantavirus cases often occur after changes in reservoir populations, rodent abundance and infection prevalence can act as early-warning indicators. Long-term ecological studies in Europe and the Americas have shown that rodent population cycles may precede changes in human disease risk [6, 7]. In China, ecologi- cal studies of HFRS have also emphasised the interacting roles of environmental variability, reservoir ecology and human behaviour in shaping disease dynamics [5]. These findings support a practical One Health implication: rodent monitoring should not be treated solely as ecolog- ical research, but as part of an integrated risk-assessment system linking animal, environmental and human health data. Land use, agriculture and human exposure: evidence from China and beyond Land use determines how often reservoir hosts, con- taminated environments and susceptible humans share the same space. Agricultural expansion, crop harvesting, grain storage, peri-domestic farming structures, forest edges and poorly sealed rural housing can increase the opportunities for contact with rodent excreta. A system- atic review of land cover, land use and human hantavi- rus infection risk found that agricultural land use was positively associated with infection risk in several set- tings, particularly in China and Brazil, whereas associa- tions with forest cover, grassland or built-up areas varied by region and virus ecology [8]. This heterogeneity is important, in that land use is not a universal risk factor but rather modifies exposure through local combinations of reservoir species, farming systems, housing conditions and human behaviour. China provides one of the clearest examples of how virus ecology and human activity jointly structure hanta- virus seasonality. In many endemic areas, HFRS shows a bimodal pattern, with a larger autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak. In China, this bimodal pattern has often been interpreted as reflect- ing the coexistence of different virus–host systems and exposure settings. Hantaan virus, mainly associated with Apodemus agrarius, contributes more to field or rural exposure and autumn–winter incidence, whereas Seoul virus, carried by Rattus norvegicus, is more relevant to peri-domestic or urban transmission and spring inci- dence in many settings [9–11]. Spatial analyses from the same region further suggested that Page 3 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 spring and autumn risks differed geographically, support- ing targeted seasonal prevention [12]. The link between agricultural activity and HFRS sea- sonality is particularly evident in high-incidence prov- inces such as Shandong. A time-series analysis reported marked seasonality and discussed the temporal cor- respondence between agricultural activity and HFRS incidence: the autumn harvest usually begins in late September, cases then rise rapidly in October, peak in November, and decline in December [13]. The incubation period of hantavirus infection suggests that this pattern is biologically plausible and consistent with exposure dur- ing harvesting, field work, grain handling or temporary accommodation in rodent-infested settings. Farmers, forestry workers, construction work- ers, cleaners, military personnel and people entering rodent-infested buildings may experience intense short- term exposure when contaminated dust is disturbed. Recreational exposure can occur when visitors stay in cabins, campsites or enclosed structures with rodent infestation. The 2012 Yosemite National Park outbreak, linked to overnight stays in insulated tent cabins, showed how built environments can convert local rodent ecology into visitor risk [14]. The 2026 cruise-associated Andes virus cluster illustrates a different pathway, with local ecological exposure potentially becoming a multi-coun- try public health problem when combined with delayed recognition, confined travel settings and international movements [15]. National surveillance has combined human case report- ing with rodent surveillance, laboratory testing and tar- geted prevention in endemic areas. During 2006–2012, 77,558 HFRS cases and 866 deaths were reported in China. Cases were clustered in a small number of prov- inces and occurring mainly in spring and autumn–win- ter seasons, with farmers remaining the largest affected occupational group [10]. These regional contrasts are summarised in Table 1, which compares rodent, envi- ronmental and human surveillance components across China, Europe and the Americas. Despite the value of long-term case reporting, human surveillance alone is inherently too late for hantavirus prevention, and human cases usually only appear after ecological changes, rodent population shifts and expo- sure events have already occurred. Clinical recogni- tion may also be delayed because the early symptoms are non-specific and overlap with leptospirosis, dengue, influenza-like illness, malaria, COVID-19 and other febrile syndromes [3]. This is particularly relevant in rural or travel-related settings, where the exposure event may be remote in time and place from the diagnosis. For surveillance to support prevention rather than only documentation, clinical signals should be connected with rodent, environmental and exposure information. In clinical practice, a compatible syndrome combined with a carefully reconstructed exposure history—such as recent rural residence, crop harvesting, cleaning of rodent-infested spaces, cabin stay or expedition travel— may provide the first actionable signal before laboratory confirmation. Information on rodent density, reser- voir infection prevalence, climate anomalies, agricultural calendars, land-use changes, clinical syndromes and travel or occupational histories is often held by different sectors and interpreted separately. analysis.methods: This mini review synthesises published evidence on ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus disease through a One Health lens.
analysis.results: Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that hantavirus incidence is associated with rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land‑use, agricultural practices, housing environments and recreational or travel‑related exposure; China displays a major autumn‑winter HFRS peak and a smaller spring‑summer peak, Europe’s bank‑vole cycles influence Puumala virus epidemics, and studies in the Americas link rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings.
analysis.contribution: The authors suggest moving beyond generic multisector calls to evidence‑informed surveillance that links rodent, environmental and human data, enabling setting‑specific prevention such as seasonal risk warnings and exposure‑reduction measures before harvest periods in endemic agricultural regions.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic viruses causing HFRS in Eurasia and HCPS in the Americas, with risk influenced by reservoir ecology, climate and human exposure. Methods: This mini review synthesises evidence on ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges through a One Health lens. Results: Incidence is linked to rodent dynamics, climate, land‑use, agriculture, housing and travel exposure; China shows autumn‑winter and spring‑summer HFRS peaks, Europe’s bank‑vole cycles drive Puumala virus epidemics, and Americas studies associate rainfall, rodent abundance and varied human exposure. Contribution: Authors propose evidence‑informed, integrated surveillance linking animal, environmental and human data to enable setting‑specific prevention such as seasonal warnings and exposure‑reduction before harvest. Limitations: Limitations not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 通过 One Health 视角的出现:生态动态、人类暴露与综合监测

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒是啮齿动物传播的动物源性病毒,可导致欧亚地区的肾综合征出血热以及美洲的汉坦病毒心肺综合征,其感染风险受宿主生态、环境变异性和人类暴露的影响。
analysis_zh.methods: 本小型综述通过一体化健康视角综合已发表的证据,探讨了汉坦病毒疾病的生态驱动因素、暴露途径和监测挑战。
analysis_zh.results: 来自中国、欧洲和美洲的证据表明,汉坦病毒发病率与啮齿动物种群动态、气候条件、土地利用、农业实践、居住环境以及休闲或旅行相关的暴露有关;中国呈现出秋冬季的肾综合征出血热高峰和春夏季的较小峰值,欧洲的田鼠循环影响普马拉病毒流行,且美洲的研究将降雨、啮齿动物丰度和人类在家庭、职业和休闲环境中的暴露联系起来。
analysis_zh.contribution: 作者建议超越笼统的多部门呼吁,转向基于证据的监测,将啮齿动物、环境和人类数据关联起来,从而在流行的农业地区于收获期前实施针对特定情境的防控措施,如季节性风险预警和降低暴露的措施。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告局限性。

papers.title: Human Orthohantavirus infections: From virology and clinical epidemiology to oral biological features and dental practice
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for 2 severe clinical syndromes in humans: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), affecting an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 individuals annually worldwide, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), characterized by fulminant pulmonary edema with case fatality rates approaching 40%. Although the systemic manifestations of hantavirus disease are well described, the oral and salivary dimensions of infection have received comparatively little attention in the dental literature. This review synthesizes current evidence on the virology, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, oral complications, diagnostic approaches, treatment options, and dental practice implications of human hantavirus infections. A narrative review with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted, supplemented by hand-searching and by consultation of the World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control outbreak reporting. Particular attention was directed toward primary research on salivary immunity, oral fluid diagnostics, and salivary gland tropism. Andes virus (ANDV) antigen has been detected in secretory cells of human salivary glands, and ANDV uniquely resists the antiviral capacity of human saliva, providing a biologically plausible mechanism for its person-to-person transmissibility. Infectious virus has since been recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid during acute infection, although a salivary route of transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven. In a cohort of 69 confirmed ANDV-infected cases, salivary secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) was significantly elevated (4.846 vs. 0.333 mg/mL in exposed-uninfected contacts), whereas mucins MUC7 and MUC5B were more frequently detected in exposed-but-not-infected household contacts, a cross-sectional finding whose direction of causation is unresolved. Total salivary sIgA is a non-specific marker of mucosal immune activation and has no pathogen specificity. Oral fluid IgM assays for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity against serum reference, supporting further evaluation of non-invasive salivary surveillance. Clinically, severe sore throat persisting for 2 to 3 weeks and oropharyngeal edema are documented as early features of hantavirus infection. Thrombocytopenia, which may be profound during the oliguric phase of HFRS, confers significant oral hemorrhagic risk. Human hantavirus infection presents with clinically significant oral and salivary manifestations that are directly relevant to dental practitioners. Dental teams should be aware of the hemorrhagic risk in patients with thrombocytopenia, the aerosol risk in patients with HCPS, the theoretical risk of ANDV transmission via oral contact in endemic regions, and the emerging utility of salivary diagnostics. Recommendations for dental practice are extrapolated from medical, virological, and general infection control evidence, rather than from dental clinical research, and are identified as precautionary where that is the case.

Although the systemic manifestations of hantavirus disease are well described, the oral and salivary dimensions of infection have received comparatively little attention in the dental literature. This review synthesizes current evidence on the virology, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, oral complications, diagnostic approaches, treatment options, and dental practice implications of human hantavirus infections. A narrative review with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted, supplemented by hand-searching and by consultation of the World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control outbreak reporting. Particular attention was directed toward primary research on salivary immunity, oral fluid diagnostics, and salivary gland tropism. Andes virus (ANDV) antigen has been detected in secretory cells of human salivary glands, and ANDV uniquely resists the antiviral capacity of human saliva, providing a biologically plausible mechanism for its person-to-person transmissibility. Infectious virus has since been recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid during acute infection, although a salivary route of transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven. In a cohort of 69 confirmed ANDV-infected cases, salivary secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) was significantly elevated (4.846 vs. 0.333 mg/mL in exposed-uninfected contacts), whereas mucins MUC7 and MUC5B were more frequently detected in exposed-but-not-infected household contacts, a cross-sectional finding whose direction of causation is unresolved. Total salivary sIgA is a non-specific marker of mucosal immune activation and has no pathogen specificity. Oral fluid IgM assays for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity against serum reference, supporting further evaluation of non-invasive salivary surveillance. Clinically, severe sore throat persisting for 2 to 3 weeks and oropharyngeal edema are documented as early features of hantavirus infection. Thrombocytopenia, which may be profound during the oliguric phase of HFRS, confers significant oral hemorrhagic risk. Human hantavirus infection presents with clinically significant oral and salivary manifestations that are directly relevant to dental practitioners. Dental teams should be aware of the hemorrhagic risk in patients with thrombocytopenia, the aerosol risk in patients with HCPS, the theoretical risk of ANDV transmission via oral contact in endemic regions, and the emerging utility of salivary diagnostics. Recommendations for dental practice are extrapolated from medical, virological, and general infection control evidence, rather than from dental clinical research, and are identified as precautionary where that is the case.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (150,000‑200,000 cases annually) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with case‑fatality rates up to 40%, representing a major public‑health concern. (A1)
analysis.methods: The authors conducted a narrative review with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, supplemented by hand‑searching and WHO/ECDC outbreak reports. (A4)
analysis.results: ANDV antigen was detected in secretory cells of human salivary glands and infectious virus recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid, suggesting possible oral shedding (A6, A7). In a cohort of 69 confirmed ANDV cases, salivary sIgA was markedly elevated (4.846 mg/mL) versus exposed‑uninfected contacts (0.333 mg/mL) (A8). An oral‑fluid IgM assay for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7 % sensitivity and 94.9 % specificity against serum reference (A11).
analysis.contribution: The review identifies oral and salivary manifestations relevant to dental practice, highlights hemorrhagic and aerosol transmission risks, and proposes salivary diagnostics as a non‑invasive surveillance tool. (A14, A15)
analysis.limitations: Recommendations are extrapolated from non‑dental evidence and are precautionary; the work is an abstract‑only narrative review lacking primary dental research data. (A16)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS (150,000‑200,000 cases/year) and HCPS with up to 40% fatality, a major health issue. Methods: A narrative review used structured searches of major databases and WHO/ECDC reports. Results: ANDV antigen was found in salivary glands and infectious virus recovered from saliva; sIgA was higher in 69 infected cases (4.846 vs 0.333 mg/mL); oral‑fluid IgM assay showed 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity. Contribution: Highlights oral manifestations, transmission risks for dentists, and potential of salivary diagnostics. Limitations: Recommendations are precautionary, based on non‑dental evidence, and the article is abstract‑only.

analysis_zh.methods: 作者进行了一项叙述性综述,采用结构化检索 PubMed/MEDLINE、Scopus、Web of Science 和 Google Scholar,并辅以手工检索及 WHO/ECDC 疫情报告。(A4)
analysis_zh.contribution: 本综述指出与牙科实践相关的口腔和唾液表现,强调出血性和气溶胶传播风险,并提出将唾液诊断作为非侵入性监测工具。(A14, A15)
analysis_zh.limitations: 建议基于非牙科证据进行推断,属预防性;本工作仅为摘要型叙述性综述,缺乏原始牙科研究数据。(A16)

papers.title: Multi-host circulation and evolutionary dynamics of hantaviruses in small mammals in Southwestern China
papers.abstract: China represents a major hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS)-endemic region, where small mammals, particularly rodents, constitute the principal reservoir hosts. This study characterized HV diversity, RNA detection rate, host range, evolutionary history, and tissue distribution in 1 717 wild small mammals collected from Yunnan Province, China. HVs were detected in 47 animals, corresponding to an overall RNA detection rate of 2.74% (47/1 717, 95% CI: 1.97%–3.51%). At least five HV species or lineages were identified across 10 small mammal species, including Orthohantavirus luxiense (LUXV), Orthohantavirus fugongense (FUGV), Orthohantavirus seoulense (SEOV), Orthohantavirus caobangense (CBNV), and Thottimvirus sp. Host‐virus coevolutionary analysis suggested extensive interspecies transmission, with particularly strong support for phylogenetically inferred host‐switching events involving SEOV and FUGV. Preliminary analysis of tissue viral loads revealed that LUXV was widely distributed across various tissues and that significant differences in viral levels existed among tissues (χ2 = 27.500, P < 0.001). Collectively, these findings elucidate the genetic diversity and evolutionary dynamics of HVs in small mammals in Yunnan.

Preliminary analysis of tissue viral loads revealed that LUXV was widely distributed across various tissues and that significant differences in viral levels existed among tissues (χ2 = 27.500, P < 0.001). Collectively, these findings elucidate the genetic diversity and evolutionary dynamics of HVs in small mammals in Yunnan. papers.title: Vaccines Against Hantavirus Infections: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hantaviruses infections are responsible for a hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome with case-fatality rates up to 50%. While inactivated vaccines are already available in China and South Korea, several additional candidate vaccines are under development. This systematic review summarizes the current clinical evidence on immunogenicity and short-term safety of vaccines targeting different hantavirus strains. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic literature search was carried out to identify randomized and nonrandomized trials of any phase. Data were synthesized narratively within strata defined by vaccine platform, target virus, assay, immunogenicity and safety. Results: Ten trials on 961 adults were included: four single-arm trials on the inactivated vaccine and six early-phase DNA-vaccine trials. One month after last dose, the inactivated vaccine achieved neutralizing seropositivity by PRNT50 in 45.1% of the tested subjects after two priming doses and 55.7% after three, while the corresponding binding-antibody values measured by IFA were 87.3% and 95.7%. Among DNA vaccines, homologous responses reached 100% against HTNV and 83.3% against PUUV with monovalent constructs, whereas dual responses to the bivalent construct were registered in 33.3% and 77.8% of the subjects, when measured through PRNT50 and PsVNA50, respectively. One serious adverse event occurred, most likely unrelated to vaccination. Conclusions: No serious safety signal was identified, although safety remains insufficiently characterized. Measured immunogenicity depends as much on the assay as on the vaccine, and, in the absence of a validated correlate of protection, it cannot be read as a clinical benefit. Future research should prioritize validated correlates of protection and innovative trial designs adapted to low-incidence diseases.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome and can have case‑fatality rates up to 50% (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The review examines licensed inactivated vaccines in China/South Korea and a range of DNA vaccine candidates, organized by platform, target virus, assay, immunogenicity and safety (A2).
analysis.current_state: Ten trials involving 961 adults show modest neutralizing seropositivity for inactivated vaccines and variable responses for DNA vaccines, with no clear serious safety signal (A3).
analysis.gaps: Immunogenicity results are assay‑dependent and, without a validated correlate of protection, cannot be interpreted as clinical benefit; safety data remain insufficiently characterized (A11).
analysis.future_research: Future work should focus on defining validated correlates of protection and employing innovative trial designs adapted to the low‑incidence nature of hantavirus disease (A12).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infections cause severe hemorrhagic fever with up to 50% fatality (A1). Main directions: Review covers existing inactivated vaccines and DNA vaccine candidates, stratified by platform, target virus, and assay (A2). Current state: Ten trials (961 adults) show modest neutralizing responses and no serious safety signals (A3). Gaps: Lack of validated protection correlates and limited safety data hinder clinical interpretation (A11). Future research: Prioritize correlates of protection and innovative low‑incidence trial designs (A12).

papers.title_zh: 针对 汉坦病毒 感染的疫苗:系统文献综述

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 感染导致肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征,死亡率最高可达 50%(A1)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述评估了中国/韩国已获许可的灭活疫苗以及一系列 DNA 疫苗候选者,按平台、靶向病毒、检测方法、免疫原性和安全性进行组织(A2)。
analysis_zh.current_state: 十项涉及 961 名成人的试验显示灭活疫苗的中度中和抗体阳性率,DNA 疫苗的反应多变,且未出现明显严重安全信号(A3)。

papers.title: Transmission timing and containment risk in human Andes virus outbreaks
papers.abstract: Abstract The 2026 multinational Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina triggered extensive contact tracing and quarantine. Whether intervention on this scale was necessary or sufficient depends on the risk of onward transmission, which can be difficult to estimate early in an outbreak. Using transmission-pair data from the 2018–2019 outbreak in Epuyén, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5–19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyén-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. These findings therefore support rapid, comprehensive contact tracing and quarantine after large international exposure events despite substantial costs.

Introduction Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus known to be capable of person-to-person transmission, although documented transmission has been confined to a small number of localized outbreaks [1– 3]. ANDV infection is associated with a case-fatality rate of approximately 36% [4], and there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral therapies. Recent increases in ANDV activity in South America have heightened concern about the potential for person-to-person spread [5]. In 2026, a multinational ANDV exposure event linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina led to 13 reported cases and 3 deaths, and prompted extensive international contact tracing and prolonged quarantine of 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries [6, 7]. The severity of ANDV disease and its potential for person-to-person spread may warrant such intensive responses, but evidence on their effectiveness and associated quarantine burden remains limited. Evaluating containment strategies requires a detailed understanding of ANDV transmission dy- namics. Decisions about the scale and duration of contact tracing and quarantine depend on incu- bation periods, the timing of infectiousness relative to symptom onset, and individual-level variation in transmission. Long incubation periods prolong monitoring and quarantine, transmission before symptom onset allows infected individuals to spread infection before they are recognized and iso- lated, and variation in transmission means that a small number of infected individuals may account for a disproportionate share of secondary infections. However, estimating these quantities from outbreak data is complicated by evolving control measures, including case detection, isolation, and quarantine, which alter transmission opportunities over time. The 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak provides the most detailed empirical data on person-to-person ANDV transmission. The original outbreak investigation reconstructed transmission chains, identi- fied superspreading, and estimated that the effective reproduction number (Re) declined from 2.12 before implementation of isolation and quarantine to 0.96 afterward [13]. Most reported ANDV infections, by contrast, arise from zoonotic spillover and are not followed by sustained person-to- person transmission. Transmission in Epuyén concentrated at a birthday party and a wake, in a town of fewer than 2,000 people, suggesting that what distinguishes these outcomes is not where infection is acquired but the number and intensity of close contacts during the brief window around symptom onset, variation in infectiousness across individuals, or both. The relative contributions of contact and infectiousness cannot be resolved from existing investigations, which report secondary cases but not contacts that did not result in transmission. Because incubation can last several weeks, the setting an infected person occupies during the transmission window may differ substan- tially from the setting in which exposure occurred. Transmission potential can therefore vary among cases, locations, and generations of the same outbreak. More recently, a latent-time analysis of the Epuyén transmission-pair data jointly estimated unobserved infection times, generation intervals, transmission timing relative to source symptom onset, time-varying reproduction numbers, and offspring dispersion from interval-censored data [12]. However, it modeled incubation and transmission timing as separate empirical delay distributions rather than as outcomes of a shared within-host process. This limited its ability to represent 2 .
