Genomics & Informatics (2026) 24:19 1 Introduction Nephropathia epidemica (NE) is attributed to Puumala virus (PUUV), a naturally occurring form of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in humans, which is a zoonotic infectious disease and generally considered a mild-to-moderate form of hantavirus infection within the HFRS spectrum [1–4]. PUUV (Puumala orthohantavi- rus) is classified within the genus Orthohantavirus, fam- ily Hantaviridae, and order Bunyavirales, as defined by current ICTV taxonomy, and it was previously grouped under the family Bunyaviridae prior to taxonomic reclas- sification [5, 6]. PUUV infection presents with highly variable out- comes, ranging from subclinical cases (70–80%) to severe HFRS, and carries a fatality rate of about 0.1% [7]. PUUV infection commonly presents with sudden fever, head- ache, back pain, nausea, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, hematuria, and varying degrees of acute kidney impairment [1, 8]. In some patients, addi- tional manifestations such as blurred vision, dizziness, insomnia, respiratory complications, oliguria, and sub- sequent polyuria during recovery may also occur [2, 9]. Although PUUV infection is generally considered mild, severe complications can occur in a subset of patients, including acute kidney failure, hypotension, shock, pul- monary edema, Guillain-Barré syndrome, respiratory distress, disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), myocarditis, encephalitis, pituitary hemorrhage, seizures, and, in rare cases, multiorgan failure or fatal cerebral hemorrhage [2, 3, 10, 11]. The first identification of PUUV occurred in the early 1980s when the virus was isolated from bank voles (Myodes glareolus) in the Puumala region of Finland [2]. Between July 1989 and June 1996, Finland reported 6701 PUUV infection cases confirmed via serologi- cal assays, with the highest incidence in the Itä-Savo district and a mortality rate below 0.1%, and later from 1995 to 2008, 22,681 cases were recorded with an average annual incidence of 31 per 100,000 population, resulting in 13 deaths and 52% of patients requiring hospitaliza- tion [12, 13]. PUUV accounts for approximately 93% of all notified hantavirus infections in Germany and caused a major outbreak in 2007 in Baden-Württemberg with 1089 reported human cases, while the highest annual number of PUUV infections in Germany was recorded in 2010 since hantavirus surveillance began in 2001 [14, 15]. Also in 2007, Sweden’s Västerbotten County experi- enced a surprisingly severe outbreak of PUUV infection, with NE rates hitting 313 cases per 100,000 residents [16, 17]. Between 2001 and 2017, a total of 12,148 hantavirus disease cases were recorded, of which 9714 (approxi- mately 97.41%) were attributed to PUUV infection [18]. In 2019, Europe recorded over 4000 hantavirus cases (0.8 per 100,000), 98% caused by PUUV, with Finland and Germany making up 69% of the total [19]. From 2018 to 2025, Hungary recorded 51 lab-confirmed hantavirus infections, 20 of which were specifically linked to the PUUV [20]. In Finland, between 560 and 3800 cases of NE are reported each year, though the actual number is believed to be nearly six times higher [21]. PUUV is a spherical enveloped pathogen character- ized by a segmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome [5, 21]. The PUUV possesses a tripartite genome: the L segment (~ 6.5 kb) encodes a ~ 2156-amino-acid L protein (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) with replicase, transcriptase, and endo- nuclease functions; the M segment (~ 3.7 kb) encodes a ~ 1148-amino-acid glycoprotein precursor that is co- translationally cleaved into Gn (70 kDa) and Gc (55 kDa); and the S segment (~ 1.8 kb) encodes a ~ 433-amino-acid nucleocapsid (N) protein [2, 5, 22, 23]. Gc is the protein that mediates fusion by the identification of a peptide of fusion, whereas Gn serves as a folding chaperone for Gc and controls the time of fusion; both are necessary for the virus to adhere as well as enter host cells [2, 24]. Gn and Gc form the principal antigenic surface of PUUV and are major targets of neutralizing antibodies, contributing to protective immunity and vaccine relevance [25–27]. The N protein plays multiple roles in viral genome transport, replication, and assembly through its interactions with host cellular proteins, while also acting as a highly immu- nogenic viral component in both humans and animal models [28, 29]. The N protein is highly conserved among orthohantaviruses and elicits a strong early antibody response during acute infection, making it an important target for both diagnostic applications and vaccine devel- opment [30, 31]. Various vaccine platforms are available, each possess- ing distinct advantages and drawbacks. For example, live attenuated vaccines trigger strong, long-lasting immu- nity but can be risky for immunocompromised individu- als due to possible reversion to virulence; inactivated vaccines are safer and more stable, though they usually require multiple doses; subunit vaccines use only key antigens, lowering the chance of side effects, but often need adjuvants and booster shots to achieve durable pro- tection [32–35]. Moreover, DNA vaccines offer rapid, stable, and cost-effective production with long-lasting immunity, but they often show weak immunogenicity in humans and face delivery challenges [34, 36]. In con- trast, the key advantage of mRNA vaccines lies in their rapid design and production, enabling swift responses to emerging infections and pandemic threats without the need to culture live pathogens [37, 38]. In recognition of these advances, the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine honored Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman Page 3 of 26 Hossain et al. Genomics & Informatics (2026) 24:19 for their groundbreaking contributions to nucleoside engineering, a key innovation that enabled the successful development of mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 [39]. Recent developments in bioinformatics have improved biopharmaceutical design by enabling rapid prediction of protein features, structural modeling, and immuno- genicity assessment. These computational approaches accelerate the identification and optimization of thera- peutic candidates while reducing time and experimental costs; however, challenges related to prediction accuracy, biological complexity, and the need for experimental validation remain important considerations [40]. Reverse vaccinology (RV) applies bioinformatics and immuno- informatics to screen microbial genomes for conserved, immunogenic epitopes, enabling faster, safer, and cost- effective vaccine development compared to traditional pathogen culturing, a slow and labor-intensive process [41, 42]. Vaccine development against PUUV infection has included inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recom- binant subunit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccines [43–45]. Among these, inactivated and DNA vaccine candidates have demon- strated promising immunogenicity in preclinical studies [44–46]. Currently, no vaccine has been authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for PUUV infection [9, 47]. Several studies have suggested the potential of multi- epitope vaccine approaches using immunoinformatics- based strategies. Khan et al. developed a multi-epitope vaccine candidate against SARS-CoV-2 by integrating epitope prediction, antigenicity assessment, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response analysis, demonstrating the feasibility of com- putational vaccine design approaches [48]. Similarly, Peele et al. designed a multi-epitope vaccine construct containing predicted B-cell and T-cell epitopes and evaluated its structural and immunological proper- ties through computational analyses [49]. These studies highlighted the potential of combining multiple immune targets within a single vaccine construct; however, their findings remained primarily dependent on computa- tional predictions and required experimental validation to confirm immunogenicity and protective efficacy. However, despite these advances, several challenges remain in current multi-epitope vaccine development strategies. Computational vaccine designs are depend- ent on prediction algorithms, reference databases, structural modeling assumptions, and available biologi- cal information, which may influence the reliability of predicted vaccine candidates. In addition, variations in epitope selection criteria, antigen conservation analysis, population coverage evaluation, and structural validation approaches can affect the effectiveness of computational vaccine design. Recent studies have emphasized that although immunoinformatics approaches accelerate multi-epitope vaccine development, comprehensive experimental validation remains essential for confirming biological relevance and protective potential [50]. Despite previous vaccine development efforts, includ- ing inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recombinant subu- nit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccine candidates, no PUUV vaccine has currently received regulatory approval. An integrated mRNA multi-epitope vaccine strategy targeting con- served regions of both PUUV glycoproteins (Gn/Gc) and nucleocapsid protein remains insufficiently explored. A comprehensive framework combining conserved antigen identification, multi-epitope vaccine construction, struc- tural evaluation, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction for PUUV has not been extensively investigated. Therefore, this study aimed to design and evaluate the PV-GNProtecta vaccine candidate using an integrated immunoinfor- matics workflow involving conserved antigen identifica- tion, epitope prediction, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction. The findings provide computational insights into the potential characteristics of PV-GNPro- tecta while recognizing the necessity of experimental val- idation for future assessment. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Acquisition and characterization of viral protein sequences The UniProt protein database (https://​www.​unipr​ot.​org/; accessed on 15 July 2025) was used for obtaining amino acid sequences of the target proteins from PUUV of G (accession number: P41266) and N (accession numbers: P41270) [51]. The G and N proteins were selected due to their key roles in PUUV infection and immune recogni- tion. The G protein mediates viral attachment and entry and is a major target of neutralizing antibodies, whereas the highly conserved N protein contributes to viral repli- cation and induces strong immune responses. Compared with the intracellular RdRp/L protein, G and N provide more suitable targets for antibody and cellular immune responses. A comparative evaluation of these proteins is provided in Supplementary Table S14. 2.2 Physicochemical and structural characterization of selected proteins The selected PUUV G and N proteins were character- ized for signal peptide presence, transmembrane regions, and subcellular localization. Signal peptide predic- tion was performed using SignalP 6.0 (https://​servi​ces.​ healt​htech.​dtu.​dk/​servi​ces/​Signa​lP-6.​0/; accessed on 15 Page 4 of 26 Hossain et al. Genomics & Informatics (2026) 24:19 September 2026) with the organism group selected as Eukarya and the default prediction model [52]. Trans- membrane topology was predicted using DeepTMHMM version 1.0.57 (accessed on 15 September 2026) using the default settings [53]. Subcellular localization informa- tion was obtained from UniProt (https://​www.​unipr​ot.​ org/; accessed on 15 September 2026) based on available curated annotations [54]. 2.3 Analysis of multiple sequence alignment and evolutionary relationships To support RV analysis, the sequence is encoded using amino acid residue codes and preserved as a FASTA sequence file. The acquired sequences were subsequently utilized for multiple sequence alignment (MSA) through the Clustal Omega platform (https://​www.​ebi.​ac.​uk/​ jdisp​atcher/​msa/​clust​alo; accessed on 05 August 2025) [55]. The Mega X tool (https://​www.​megas​oftwa​re.​net/; accessed on 05 August 2025) was employed for phyloge- netic analysis on both genomes [56]. 2.4 Prediction of epitopes for MHC I, MHC II, and linear B‐cell interactions The MHC I epitopes from the G and N proteins were found using the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) (http://​tools.​iedb.​org/​mhci/; accessed on 20 August 2025) software, with a percentile rank < 1.00 as the selec- tion criterion [57]. This tool is a sophisticated database comprising information on MHC molecules, T-cell and B-cell epitopes, antibodies, and MHC-binding ligands identified in humans and various animal taxonomic groups, including primates and rodents [58, 59]. A cut- off percentile rank of less than 1.00 was implemented for epitope selection, which suggests that the binding affinity was improved [37]. Lower percentile rank values indicate stronger predicted peptide–MHC binding affin- ity [60]. The IEDB (http://​tools.​iedb.​org/​mhcii/; accessed on 20 August 2025) was applied to forecast the MHC II epitopes inside the designated areas of these proteins, and peptides with percentile ranks < 1.00 were considered potential high-affinity binders and selected for further evaluation [61]. Subsequently, the human allele reference sets were employed to predict CD8 + and CD4 + bind- ing. The ABCpred tool (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​ va/​abcpr​ed/; accessed on 25 August 2025) was used to estimate the continuous B-cell epitopes of the selected portions of these proteins. This tool provides epitope predictions by analyzing the sequence features of the tar- get antigens [58, 62]. This program uses an affinity scale method based on a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to predict continuous B-cell epitopes [63, 64]. Additionally, the MHC-II epitopes underwent some additional analy- ses, including IL-10 (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​ il10p​red/; accessed on 25 September 2026), IFN-gamma (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​ifnep​itope/​predi​ct.​ php; accessed on 25 September 2026), IL-2 (https://​webs.​ iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​il2pr​ed/; accessed on 25 September 2026) and IL-4 (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​il4pr​ ed/​design.​php; accessed on 25 September 2026) by using the respective servers. Between 2001 and 2017, a total of 12,148 hantavirus disease cases were recorded, of which 9714 (approxi- mately 97.41%) were attributed to PUUV infection [18]. In 2019, Europe recorded over 4000 hantavirus cases (0.8 per 100,000), 98% caused by PUUV, with Finland and Germany making up 69% of the total [19]. From 2018 to 2025, Hungary recorded 51 lab-confirmed hantavirus infections, 20 of which were specifically linked to the PUUV [20]. In Finland, between 560 and 3800 cases of NE are reported each year, though the actual number is believed to be nearly six times higher [21]. PUUV is a spherical enveloped pathogen character- ized by a segmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome [5, 21]. The PUUV possesses a tripartite genome: the L segment (~ 6.5 kb) encodes a ~ 2156-amino-acid L protein (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) with replicase, transcriptase, and endo- nuclease functions; the M segment (~ 3.7 kb) encodes a ~ 1148-amino-acid glycoprotein precursor that is co- translationally cleaved into Gn (70 kDa) and Gc (55 kDa); and the S segment (~ 1.8 kb) encodes a ~ 433-amino-acid nucleocapsid (N) protein [2, 5, 22, 23]. papers.title: Framing the 2026 Global Hantavirus Outbreak in Nigerian Online Newspapers: Insights from Premium Times and Sahara Reporters
papers.abstract: Background: Emerging infectious diseases often attract significant media attention because of their potential impact on public health perceptions and preparedness. Despite the absence of confirmed cases in Nigeria, the 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak generated global public health concern because of increased international mobility and the potential risk of cross-border transmission. Objective: This study investigated how Premium Times and Sahara Reporters framed the 2026 global hantavirus outbreak, focusing on the frequency, presentation formats, prominence, and dominant frames of coverage. Method: The study employed a content analysis design. Using census approach, all hantavirus-related stories published by Premium Times and Sahara Reporters between 2 and 30 May 2026 were identified, yielding 29 stories for analysis. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, while Holsti’s (1969) formula was used to assess inter-coder reliability, yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.85. Results: Premium Times published 17 stories (58.6%), while Sahara Reporters published 12 stories (41.4%). Of the 29 stories, 24 (82.8%) were news stories, 19 (65.5%) received low prominence, and 10 (34.5%) adopted a health risk/awareness frame, followed by the prevention and safety measures frame (5 stories; 17.2%) and the attribution of responsibility frame (4 stories; 13.8%). Conclusion: Nigerian online newspapers reported the outbreak primarily as a public health risk but devoted limited attention and prominence to the issue, suggesting a predominantly reactive orientation in the newspapers' reporting of emerging health threats. Unique Contribution: This study contributes empirical evidence on Nigerian media framing of the 2026 global hantavirus outbreak and extends health communication scholarship on emerging zoonotic diseases. Key Recommendation: Nigerian online newspapers should adopt more sustained, prominent, explanatory, and interpretative reporting of emerging infectious diseases to strengthen public preparedness and risk communication.
authors: Valentine Okwudilichukwu Ezema, Sunday Uche Aja, Mercy Ifeyinwa Obichili, Joseph N. Chukwu, Chika Thonia Ezeali, Ijeoma Njideka Taiwo & Kelvin Chinemerem Nkwuda

papers.title: Human febrile illness associated with Yanggou tick virus: Clinical characteristics and epidemiological links to rodents.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: We identified Yanggou tick virus (YGTV), a segmented flavivirus previously unrecognized as a human pathogen, in a patient presenting with fever and headache. This study aims to characterize the epidemiology and clinical manifestations of YGTV infection in patients with fever of unknown origin (FUO). METHODS: We conducted a surveillance study at the First Hospital of Jilin University (2020-2025) involving 1011 patients with FUO. Concurrently, ticks and rodents in the vicinity of the patients' residences and workplaces were collected for viral detection. YGTV infection was confirmed via PCR assays. Positive samples were used for viral isolation, genome amplification, and phylogenetic characterization. An Apodemus agrarius challenge model was established to evaluate viral persistence and shedding. RESULTS: Of the 30 confirmed cases of YGTV infection, 10 were co-diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). The patients showed no clear seasonality or geographic bias. Notably, rodent contact (43.3%) was a more frequent risk factor than tick bites (6.7%). While clinical presentations were non-specific, nearly 50% of the patients presented with gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms. YGTV was isolated from patients, ticks, and A. agrarius (the latter often co-infected with Hantaan virus). Animal models confirmed persistent splenic infection and viral shedding via oral and fecal routes. CONCLUSION: Our findings establish YGTV as an underdiagnosed cause of human febrile illness, underscoring the transmission risks posed by tick vectors and rodent reservoirs. These results highlight the urgent need for enhanced clinical surveillance and diagnostic screening among patients presenting with FUO, particularly in regions where the virus is endemic.

analysis.background: Yanggou tick virus (YGTV) is a segmented flavivirus previously unrecognized as a human pathogen, identified in a patient presenting with fever and headache.
analysis.methods: A surveillance study (2020‑2025) of 1011 fever‑of‑unknown‑origin patients at the First Hospital of Jilin University used PCR to confirm YGTV; ticks and rodents near patients' homes were collected for viral detection; positive samples underwent isolation, genome amplification, and phylogenetic analysis; an Apodemus agrarius challenge model evaluated viral persistence and shedding.
analysis.results: Thirty YGTV infections were confirmed, including 10 co‑diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome; no clear seasonality or geographic bias was observed; rodent contact (43.3%) was more common than tick bites (6.7%); about half of patients had gastrointestinal or neurological symptoms; YGTV was isolated from patients, ticks and A. agrarius (often co‑infected with Hantaan virus); animal models showed persistent splenic infection and oral/fecal shedding.
analysis.contribution: The work establishes YGTV as an underdiagnosed cause of human febrile illness and highlights transmission risks from both tick vectors and rodent reservoirs, urging enhanced clinical surveillance and diagnostic screening in endemic regions.

analysis.summary_en: Background: YGTV is a segmented flavivirus previously unrecognized as a human pathogen, identified in a febrile patient. Methods: Surveillance of 1011 FUO patients (2020‑2025) with PCR confirmation, concurrent tick/rodent collection, viral isolation, genome sequencing, phylogenetics, and an Apodemus agrarius model assessed persistence and shedding. Results: 30 cases confirmed (10 with HFRS), no seasonality/geographic bias, rodent contact 43.3% vs tick bites 6.7%, ~50% had GI or neurological symptoms; YGTV isolated from patients, ticks, and A. agrarius (often co‑infected with Hantaan virus); animal models showed splenic persistence and oral/fecal shedding. Contribution: Establishes YGTV as an underdiagnosed febrile illness agent, highlighting tick and rodent transmission risks and the need for enhanced surveillance. Limitations: Only abstract data are provided, restricting detail on methods and broader conclusions.

papers.title_zh: 与羊沟蜱病毒相关的人类发热疾病:临床特征及与啮齿动物的流行病学关联

analysis_zh.background: Yanggou蜱病毒(YGTV)是一种分段黄病毒,之前未被认定为人类病原体,已在出现发热和头痛的患者中被鉴定。
analysis_zh.methods: 一项2020-2025年在吉林大学第一医院对1011例未知来源发热患者进行的监测研究,使用PCR确认YGTV;收集患者家附近的蜱和啮齿动物进行病毒检测;阳性样本进行分离、基因组扩增和系统发育分析;使用Apodemus agrarius挑战模型评估病毒持续性和排泄。
analysis_zh.results: 确认30例YGTV感染,其中10例与肾综合征出血热共诊断;未观察到明显的季节性或地理偏倚;啮齿动物接触(43.3%)比蜱叮咬(6.7%)更常见;约一半患者出现胃肠或神经系统症状;YGTV从患者、蜱和A. agrarius(常与汉滩病毒共感染)中分离;动物模型显示脾脏持续感染和口腔/粪便排泄。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该工作确立了YGTV作为人类发热性疾病的被低估病因,并强调了蜱媒介和啮齿动物宿主的传播风险,呼吁在流行地区加强临床监测和诊断筛查。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要信息,限制了对研究设计、统计分析和更广泛适用性的详细说明。

papers.title: Hantavirus in Dentistry: Occupational Exposure Considerations and a Proposed Tiered Infection Prevention and Control Framework-A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Objective The aim of this study is to synthesize evidence on hantavirus transmission and occupational exposure pathways relevant to dentistry, and to propose an evidence-informed tiered infection prevention and control (IPC) framework that distinguishes established from theoretical risk. Material and methods The initial narrative search covered database inception through May 15, 2026 in MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and WHO/CDC/ECDC/OSHA sources, followed by a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE and public-health guidance update through August 18, 2026. Approximately 1450 records were identified. After duplicate removal, 1070 records were subjected to title/abstract screening, 215 full-text records were assessed for eligibility, and 45 sources were included in the final synthesis, comprising 34 peer-reviewed publications and 11 gray-literature or public-health guidance sources. Results Environmental exposure to infected-rodent contamination is the established occupational pathway. Limited person-to-person transmission is documented for the Andes virus (ANDV), but no dental transmission has been reported. ANDV RNA and culture-based infectivity have been demonstrated in some oral/respiratory fluids; however, dental-aerosol transmission has not been shown. Dental-specific occupational risk therefore remains unquantified. Conclusions No dental transmission has been documented, and patient-related risk remains uncertain. Standard precautions and rodent control are foundational; suspected or confirmed ANDV warrants transmission-based precautions and airborne precautions for aerosol-generating procedures according to current guidance. The proposed dental tiers are evidence-informed, author-derived, and unvalidated.

After duplicate removal, 1070 records were subjected to title/abstract screening, 215 full-text records were assessed for eligibility, and 45 sources were included in the final synthesis, comprising 34 peer-reviewed publications and 11 gray-literature or public-health guidance sources. Results Environmental exposure to infected-rodent contamination is the established occupational pathway. Limited person-to-person transmission is documented for the Andes virus (ANDV), but no dental transmission has been reported. ANDV RNA and culture-based infectivity have been demonstrated in some oral/respiratory fluids; however, dental-aerosol transmission has not been shown. Dental-specific occupational risk therefore remains unquantified. Conclusions No dental transmission has been documented, and patient-related risk remains uncertain. Standard precautions and rodent control are foundational; suspected or confirmed ANDV warrants transmission-based precautions and airborne precautions for aerosol-generating procedures according to current guidance. The proposed dental tiers are evidence-informed, author-derived, and unvalidated.

papers.title: DNA and mRNA Vaccines Against Hantaviruses: Antigen Design, Delivery Strategies and Translational Progress.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are members of the Hantaviridae family, which can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). At present, no specific antiviral treatment is available for hantavirus infection, while licensed hantavirus vaccines are restricted to a limited number of countries in Asia. This review summarizes recent advances in hantavirus deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines, focusing on antigen design, delivery systems, immunogenicity, safety and translational development. Peer-reviewed studies published primarily within the past 10 years were evaluated together with available hantavirus vaccine trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov, with emphasis on Hantaan virus (HTNV), Puumala virus (PUUV) and Andes virus (ANDV). DNA vaccine candidates have demonstrated immunogenicity in preclinical and early clinical studies, with an acceptable safety profile. mRNA vaccines represent a newer approach with promising preclinical evidence of humoral and cellular immune responses. However, they have not yet been evaluated clinically. Studies have also reported the potential for varying degrees of cross-protection between hantavirus species, although protection remains limited by antigenic diversity. Overall, current evidence supports further development of nucleic acid-based hantavirus vaccines, particularly multivalent strategies, with emphasis on standardized evaluation and clinical efficacy.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, and no specific antivirals exist while licensed vaccines are limited to a few Asian countries. (A1, A2)
analysis.main_directions: The review surveys DNA and mRNA vaccine platforms, detailing antigen design, delivery systems, immunogenicity, safety, and translational progress, with focus on HTNV, PUUV, and ANDV. (A3, A4)
analysis.current_state: DNA vaccine candidates have demonstrated immunogenicity and acceptable safety in preclinical and early clinical studies; mRNA vaccines show strong humoral and cellular responses in preclinical models but have not yet been evaluated clinically. (A5, A6, A7)
analysis.gaps: mRNA vaccines lack clinical trial data, cross‑protection is constrained by antigenic diversity, and standardized efficacy assessments across platforms are missing. (A7, A8, A9)
analysis.future_research: Priority should be given to multivalent nucleic‑acid vaccines, development of standardized immunogenicity assays, and rigorous clinical efficacy trials across diverse hantavirus species. (A9)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe disease and lack specific antivirals, with few licensed vaccines. Main directions: The review covers DNA and mRNA vaccine design, delivery, immunogenicity, safety, and translational steps, focusing on HTNV, PUUV, ANDV. Current state: DNA vaccines are immunogenic and safe in early studies; mRNA vaccines show promising preclinical immunity but no clinical data. Gaps: No clinical evaluation of mRNA vaccines, limited cross‑protection due to antigenic diversity, and lack of standardized efficacy metrics. Future research: Advance multivalent nucleic‑acid vaccines, create uniform immunogenicity assays, and conduct definitive clinical trials across hantavirus species.

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒导致肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征,且目前没有特效抗病毒药物,已获许可的疫苗仅限于少数亚洲国家。(A1, A2)
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述调查DNA和mRNA疫苗平台,详细阐述抗原设计、递送系统、免疫原性、安全性以及转化进展,重点关注HTNV、PUUV和ANDV。(A3, A4)
analysis_zh.current_state: DNA疫苗候选物已在临床前和早期临床研究中显示出免疫原性和可接受的安全性;mRNA疫苗在临床前模型中表现出强烈的体液和细胞免疫应答,但尚未进行临床评估。(A5, A6, A7)
analysis_zh.gaps: mRNA疫苗缺乏临床试验数据,交叉保护受抗原多样性限制,且各平台之间缺乏标准化的疗效评估。(A7, A8, A9)
analysis_zh.future_research: 应优先研发多价核酸疫苗,开发标准化的免疫原性检测方法,并在多种汉坦病毒物种中开展严格的临床疗效试验。(A9)
